October_2020_MARS_Hydrophone_v4_monthly_.caption: October 2020 MARS Hydrophone v4 — detections per day. Oct 5-7 orca cluster (26, 22, 6 detections) matches documented CA140B and CA51A pod visits. Humpback dominant (254,546 total). Ship noise minimal — COVID lockdown. Classifier: orca_v4.

tsne_context_3season.png.caption: Perch V2 30s Gaussian-weighted context embeddings t-SNE — 3 seasons. 770 labeled windows. Orca completely separated from humpback — zero overlap vs significant overlap in raw 5s embeddings. Humpback splits into 3 sub-clusters suggesting song type or seasonal variation. Context window ±15s, σ=7.5s, center-weighted.

tsne_4season_norm.png.caption: Perch V2 embeddings t-SNE — 4 seasons: April 2018 + May 2018 + October 2020 + April 2026 (normalized). 1,199 labeled embeddings, 400 orca (219 April 2018 + 181 May 2018 confirmed). tsne_orca_events.png.caption: Perch V2 t-SNE — 4 seasons with orca events colored by month. April 2018 orca (dark green, n=219) and May 2018 orca (light green, n=181) shown separately. tsne_orca_by_day_4days_px10.png.caption: t-SNE of confirmed orca_call embeddings (Perch V2, cosine) — 4 confirmed days (Apr 13/18/25 + May 12 2018), perplexity=10, analysis (light theme). Apr 25 (evening encounter) forms a distinct cluster separated from the Apr 13 morning Bigg's event WITHIN the same month; separation is ROBUST across perplexity 10/30/50 and spans 10 recordings over ~3.5h (not a single-recording/boat artifact). Apr 18 is partially distinct. Exploratory — t-SNE distances/sizes are not meaningful. Finding #14 (extended April 2018 orca presence).

ksbw_news8_orca_invasion_monterey_spring.caption: KSBW Action News 8 (Monterey California) Reported an extraordinarily high number of orca sightings in April and May of 2018. One tour group reported seeing as many as 50 orcas in one day. April and May are when killer whales typically come to Monterey. The pods are drawn to area in search of gray whales. Biologists with the outfitters have been able to identify two of the pods in the bay this spring, one is from Alaska the other is from California. The California pod is known as Emma's pod, named for the group's matriarch. Emma's pod is called CA140s.

ksbw_news8_orca_invasion_monterey_spring.notes: Third-party news image, (c) KSBW; recorded as external corroboration only. Emma's pod hunts gray-whale calves, so their spring presence implies gray whales in the acoustic environment — ties to #13. '~50 in one day' is as-reported by KSBW (secondary source).
